F1.quote: Our programme was, then, to discover some faculty of reasoning about any theme put before us from the most generally accepted premisses that there are. For that is the essential task of the art of discussion (dialectic) and of examination (peirastic).
F1.claim: The inquiry undertook to find a faculty of reasoning from the most generally accepted premisses: the task of dialectic and of peirastic.

F2.quote: The reason of this we have explained; for this, too, was why Socrates used to ask questions and not to answer them; for he used to confess that he did not know.
F2.claim: Socrates is named in the statement of the inquiry's second task: he asked and did not answer, confessing he did not know.

F3.quote: For in the case of all discoveries the results of previous labours that have been handed down from others have been advanced bit by bit by those who have taken them on, whereas the original discoveries generally make advance that is small at first though much more useful than the development which later springs out of them.
F3.claim: Discoveries are of two kinds: those handed down from others and advanced bit by bit, and original discoveries, small at first.

F4.quote: Tisias coming next after the first founders, then Thrasymachus after Tisias, and Theodorus next to him, while several people have made their several contributions to it: and therefore it is not to be wondered at that the art has attained considerable dimensions.
F4.claim: Rhetoric grew by succession (Tisias, Thrasymachus, Theodorus) and many contributions.

F5.quote: Of this inquiry, on the other hand, it was not the case that part of the work had been thoroughly done before, while part had not. Nothing existed at all.
F5.claim: Of this inquiry it was not the case that part had been thoroughly done before and part not; nothing existed at all.

F6.quote: For the training given by the paid professors of contentious arguments was like the treatment of the matter by Gorgias.
F6.claim: The paid professors of contentious arguments trained like Gorgias.
F6.lineage: the paid teachers and the shoes (183b36–184a8)

F7.quote: And therefore the teaching they gave their pupils was ready but rough. For they used to suppose that they trained people by imparting to them not the art but its products,
F7.claim: Their teaching was ready but rough: they imparted not the art but its products.
F7.lineage: the paid teachers and the shoes (183b36–184a8)

F8.quote: for he has helped him to meet his need, but has not imparted an art to him.
F8.claim: The giver of shoes helps the need but imparts no art.
F8.lineage: the paid teachers and the shoes (183b36–184a8)

F9.quote: Moreover, on the subject of Rhetoric there exists much that has been said long ago, whereas on the subject of reasoning we had nothing else of an earlier date to speak of at all, but were kept at work for a long time in experimental researches.
F9.claim: Of rhetoric much had been said long ago; on reasoning we had nothing else of an earlier date to speak of at all, but worked long in experimental researches.

F10.quote: there must remain for all of you, or for our students, the task of extending us your pardon for the shortcomings of the inquiry, and for the discoveries thereof your warm thanks.
F10.claim: The hearers are asked for pardon for shortcomings and thanks for discoveries.

F11.quote: Aristotle’s logical works contain the earliest formal study of logic that we have.
F11.claim: Aristotle's logical works are the earliest formal study of logic extant.

F12.quote: It is therefore all the more remarkable that together they comprise a highly developed logical theory, one that was able to command immense respect for many centuries
F12.claim: They form a highly developed theory that commanded respect for centuries.

F13.quote: Kant thought that Aristotle had discovered everything there was to know about logic, and the historian of logic Prantl drew the corollary that any logician after Aristotle who said anything new was confused, stupid, or perverse.
F13.claim: Kant held Aristotle had discovered everything in logic; Prantl drew the corollary that later innovators were confused, stupid or perverse.

F14.quote: On Sophistical Refutations is a final section, or an appendix, to the Topics
F14.claim: SE is a final section or appendix of the Topics.
F14.lineage: the passage's place: the ending of SE and of the Topics

F15.quote: Aristotle’s study of sophistical arguments is contained in On Sophistical Refutations, which is actually a sort of appendix to the Topics.
F15.claim: SE contains the study of sophistical arguments and is a sort of appendix to the Topics.
F15.lineage: the passage's place: the ending of SE and of the Topics

F16.quote: In fact, we can discern in the Topics (and the Rhetoric, which Aristotle says depends on the art explained in the Topics) an art of dialectic for use in such arguments. My reconstruction of this art (which would not be accepted by all scholars) is as follows.
F16.claim: An art of dialectic can be discerned in the Topics; the reconstruction is the author's and not accepted by all.

F17.locus: §8.3.2 Dialectic That Puts to the Test
F17.quote: Its function is to examine the claims of those who say they have some knowledge, and it can be practiced by someone who does not possess the knowledge in question.
F17.claim: Peirastic examines those who claim knowledge and can be practised by one who lacks it.

F18.locus: §8.3.2 Dialectic That Puts to the Test
F18.quote: This is strongly reminiscent of Socrates’ style of interrogation, from which it is almost certainly descended.
F18.claim: Peirastic is almost certainly descended from Socrates' style of interrogation.

F19.quote: Aristotle himself traces the quest for definitions back to Socrates.
F19.claim: Aristotle traces the quest for definitions to Socrates.

F20.quote: This method is part of Aristotle’s Platonic legacy. His attitude towards it, however, is complex.
F20.claim: Division is part of Aristotle's Platonic legacy, his attitude to it complex.

F21.quote: Logic as a discipline starts with the transition from the more or less unreflective use of logical methods and argument patterns to the reflection on and inquiry into these methods and patterns and their elements, including the syntax and semantics of sentences.
F21.claim: Logic as a discipline starts where use of argument patterns becomes inquiry into them.

F22.quote: The Sophists, and later Plato (early 4th c.) displayed an interest in sentence analysis, truth, and fallacies, and Eubulides of Miletus (mid-4th c.) is on record as the inventor of both the Liar and the Sorites paradox.
F22.claim: Sophists, Plato and Eubulides worked on sentence analysis, truth, fallacies and paradoxes before Aristotle.

F23.quote: But logic as a fully systematic discipline begins with Aristotle, who systematized much of the logical inquiry of his predecessors.
F23.claim: Logic as a fully systematic discipline begins with Aristotle, who systematized much of his predecessors' logical inquiry.

F24.quote: Both Zeno of Elea (born c. 490 BCE) and Socrates (470–399) were famous for the ways in which they refuted an opponent’s view. Their methods display similarities with reductio ad absurdum, but neither of them seems to have theorized about their logical procedures.
F24.claim: Zeno and Socrates refuted by methods like reductio but seem not to have theorized them.

F25.quote: Socratic refutation was an exchange of questions and answers in which the opponents would be led, on the basis of their answers, to a conclusion incompatible with their original claim. Plato institutionalized such disputations into structured, rule-governed verbal contests that became known as dialectical argument.
F25.claim: Socratic refutation, institutionalized by Plato into rule-governed contests, became dialectical argument.

F26.quote: The development of a basic logical vocabulary for such contests indicates some reflection upon the patterns of argumentation.
F26.claim: A logical vocabulary for the contests indicates some prior reflection on argument patterns.

F27.quote: Plato’s Euthydemus contains a large collection of contemporary fallacies.

F28.quote: it is possible that the shaping of deduction and proof in Greek mathematics that begins in the later 5th century BCE served as an inspiration for Aristotle’s syllogistic.
F28.claim: Greek mathematics may have inspired the syllogistic.

F29.quote: Aristotle is the first great logician in the history of logic. His logic was taught by and large without rival from the 4th to the 19th centuries CE.
F29.claim: Aristotle is the first great logician; his logic was taught without rival into the 19th century.

F30.quote: However, by using logical advances as a criterion, we can conjecture that most of the Topics, Sophistical Refutations, Categories and Metaphysics Γ predate the De Interpretatione, which in turn predates the Prior Analytics and parts of the Posterior Analytics.
F30.claim: By logical advance, the Topics and SE are conjectured to predate De Interpretatione and the Prior Analytics.
F30.lineage: the passage's place: the ending of SE and of the Topics

F31.quote: The Topics provide a manual for participants in the contests of dialectical argument as instituted in the Academy by Plato.
F31.claim: The Topics is a manual for the dialectical contests Plato instituted in the Academy.

F32.quote: Aristotle’s Topics may thus count as the earliest surviving logical treatise. The Sophistical Refutations are the first systematic classification of fallacies,
F32.claim: The Topics may be the earliest surviving logical treatise; SE the first systematic classification of fallacies.

F33.quote: Aristotelian logic, after a great and early triumph, consolidated its position of influence to rule over the philosophical world throughout the Middle Ages up until the 19th Century.
F33.claim: Aristotelian logic ruled from an early triumph to the 19th century.

F34.quote: What we have are largely notes, written at various points in his career, for different purposes, edited and cobbled together by later followers.
F34.claim: The logical writings are largely notes, edited and cobbled together by later followers.
F34.lineage: the passage's place: the ending of SE and of the Topics

F35.quote: In a short work entitled Sophistical Refutations, Aristotle introduces a theory of logical fallacies that has been remarkably influential.
F35.claim: SE introduces a remarkably influential theory of fallacies.

F36.quote: We should note that much of this text, which deals with natural language argumentation, does not presuppose the syllogistic form.
F36.claim: Much of SE does not presuppose the syllogistic form.

F37.quote: According to Aristotle, this is the first work to treat the subject of deductive reasoning in ancient Greece (Soph. Ref., 34, 183b34 ff.).
F37.claim: According to Aristotle at 183b34 ff., SE is the first work to treat deductive reasoning in ancient Greece.

F38.quote: In it, he attempts to develop a pattern of sound and genuine reasoning in opposition to the deceptive or misleading "art of sophistry".
F38.claim: SE develops sound reasoning against the art of sophistry.

F39.quote: Besides, there is an introduction (1–2), an interlude (9–11), and a conclusion (33–34).
F39.claim: Chapters 33–34 are the conclusion of SE.
F39.lineage: the passage's place: the ending of SE and of the Topics

F40.quote: Immanuel Kant thought that there was nothing else to invent after the work of Aristotle,
F40.claim: Kant thought nothing else was to be invented after Aristotle.

F41.quote: On Sophistical Refutations (Latin: De Sophisticis Elenchis) gives a treatment of logical fallacies, and provides a key link to Aristotle's tractate on rhetoric.
F41.claim: SE treats fallacies and links to the Rhetoric.
F41.lineage: the passage's place: the ending of SE and of the Topics

F42.quote: Ockham and Scotus wrote commentaries on the Categories and Sophistical Refutations.
F42.claim: Ockham and Scotus commented on SE.

F43.locus: The Topics as related to Sophistical Refutations
F43.quote: The Sophistical Refutations is viewed by some[11] as an appendix to the Topics, inasmuch as its final section[12] appears to form an epilogue to both treatises.
F43.claim: SE's final section (183a38–184b9, n. 12; Forster, Loeb, n. 11) appears to form an epilogue to both the Topics and SE.
F43.lineage: the passage's place: the ending of SE and of the Topics

F44.quote: The treatise presents the art of dialectic - the invention and discovery of arguments in which the propositions rest upon commonly held opinions or endoxa
F44.claim: The Topics presents the art of dialectic from endoxa.
